literal: Sun Yu held that a single addition and added additions alike were both incorrect.
idiomatic: Sun Yu held that whether one cap was added or several, both approaches were wrong.

literal: The ritual libation text says, "On this auspicious month and day," and also, "Taking the correctness of the year, taking the order of the month."
idiomatic: The ritual invocation reads, "On this fortunate month and day," and again, "With the year's right season, with the month's proper order."

literal: Duke Xiang of Lu was capped in winter; Emperor Hui of Han was capped in the third month—clearly there was no fixed month.
idiomatic: Duke Xiang of Lu received the cap in winter, and Emperor Hui of Han in the third month—clear proof that no single month was prescribed.

literal: Since Later Han, when emperors received the cap of full adulthood, all did so in the first month.
idiomatic: From Later Han onward, every emperor's coming-of-age capping took place in the first month.

literal: In the second year of Xianning of Jin, in the intercalary ninth month of autumn, an envoy was sent to cap the Prince of Runan, Sima Jian—thus Jin ritual too was not necessarily at the year's beginning.
idiomatic: In Jin's second year of Xianning, during the intercalary ninth month of autumn, an envoy capped the Prince of Runan, Sima Jian—showing that Jin ritual as well need not fall at the New Year.

literal: By ritual one is capped at the temple; since Wei it was no longer done at the temple.
idiomatic: Ritual prescribed capping in the ancestral temple, but from Wei onward the ceremony was no longer held there.

literal: Yet when Emperors Wu and Hui of Jin capped the crown prince, both immediately had temple audience—this too was modeled on the ritual of being at the temple.
idiomatic: Yet when Emperors Wu and Hui capped the crown prince, each then appeared before the temple—a practice that still echoed the temple-based rite.

literal: When Emperors Mu and Xiaowu of Jin were about to be capped, they first reported to the temple with silk offerings; when finished they again had temple audience.
idiomatic: Before Emperors Mu and Xiaowu were capped, they first announced the event to the temple with silk offerings, and afterward appeared there again when the rite was complete.

literal: When Emperor Hui of Jin, as crown prince, was about to be capped, Emperor Wu presided at the imperial hall and had the Concurrent Minister of Education, Prince of Gaoyang, Gui, perform the cap addition, and the Concurrent Director of the Imperial Household and Colonel of the Colony Cavalry, Hua Yong, assist with the cap.
idiomatic: When the crown prince who would become Emperor Hui was to be capped, Emperor Wu presided from the throne hall and appointed Prince Gui of Gaoyang, serving concurrently as Minister of Education, to place the cap, with Hua Yong, concurrently Director of the Imperial Household and Colonel of the Colony Cavalry, to assist.

literal: When the emperors of Jiangzuo were about to be capped, bells and chime-stones were set up overnight, and the hundred officials took their attendant places.
idiomatic: Before an emperor south of the Yangzi was capped, bells and stone chimes were set out the night before, and the full corps of officials took their places beside him.

literal: They also beforehand spread a great couch on the hall.
idiomatic: A large couch was also laid out in advance on the hall floor.

literal: The Superintendent of the Imperial Wardrobe presented the cap, headcloth, hairpin, cap guide, and dragon robe to be given to the Attendant Within and the Regular Attendant.
idiomatic: The Superintendent of the Imperial Wardrobe brought forward the cap, headcloth, hairpin, cap guide, and dragon robe and handed them to the Attendant Within and the Regular Attendant.

literal: The Grand Commandant added the headcloth; the Grand Guardian added the cap.
idiomatic: The Grand Commandant placed the headcloth; the Grand Guardian placed the cap.

literal: When about to add the cap, the Grand Commandant knelt and read the invocation: "On this auspicious month and day, you now first receive the cap of full adulthood.
idiomatic: As the cap was about to be set on his head, the Grand Commandant knelt and read the invocation: "On this fortunate month and day, you now first receive the cap of full manhood.

literal: The emperor is reverent and dignified, thinking to extend the duties of the dragon robe.
idiomatic: Solemn is the emperor, mindful to fulfill the great office of the dragon robe.

literal: Reverently conforming to the vast Heaven, the six directions are the model.
idiomatic: In reverent accord with vast Heaven, may the six directions be your measure.

literal: Following ancestors and forefathers, forever without end.
idiomatic: Following the path of ancestors and forefathers, without end through endless time.

literal: May long life be hoped for; may this great blessing be granted.
idiomatic: May long life be your portion; may this resplendent blessing be conferred upon you.

literal: " When the cap addition was finished, the Attendant Within tied the black headband.
idiomatic: " When the cap had been placed, the Attendant Within fastened the black headband.

literal: The Attendant Within removed the crimson gauze robe and added the dragon robe.
idiomatic: The Attendant Within removed the crimson gauze garment and put on the dragon robe.

literal: When the capping was complete, the Grand Guardian led the multitude of ministers to present cups and offer longevity wishes; dukes and princes and those below three times shouted "Ten thousand years!" and then withdrew.
idiomatic: When the capping was finished, the Grand Guardian led the officials in raising cups to wish long life; princes, dukes, and all ranks below called "Ten thousand years!" three times, and then withdrew.

literal: According to the ritual protocols, only one addition of headcloth and cap.
idiomatic: According to the written protocols, only one headcloth and one cap were added.

literal: Under Song, the crown prince and territorial princes were also capped with only one addition.
idiomatic: Under the Song dynasty as well, the crown prince and territorial princes received only a single cap in the ceremony.

literal: The office had its records on this.
idiomatic: The relevant offices kept written regulations to that effect.

literal: In the tenth year of Taishi of Emperor Wu of Jin, Prince of Nangong, Cheng, was fifteen years old and by the old rule should be capped.
idiomatic: In the tenth year of Taishi under Emperor Wu of Jin, the Prince of Nangong, Cheng, turned fifteen and by established rule was due to be capped.

literal: The responsible offices deliberated and memorialized: "By ritual, at fifteen one becomes a mature youth.
idiomatic: The responsible offices debated the matter and memorialized: "By ritual, fifteen marks the age of a mature youth.

literal: A state's ruler at fifteen begets a son, to show the propriety of capping age.
idiomatic: A state's ruler fathers a son at fifteen, which shows when capping is proper.

literal: Moreover, Han and Wei sending envoys to cap the various princes was not ancient ritual.
idiomatic: Moreover, Han and Wei's practice of sending envoys to cap the feudal princes was not ancient ritual.

literal: " Thereupon it was decreed that all princes be capped at fifteen, no longer requiring an imperial command.
idiomatic: " Thereupon a rule was issued that all princes be capped at fifteen, without waiting for a separate imperial appointment.

literal: In the eleventh year of Yuanjia, the Marquis of Yingdao was about to be capped.
idiomatic: In the eleventh year of Yuanjia, the Marquis of Yingdao was approaching his capping ceremony.

literal: An edict said: "The Marquis of Yingdao, Yiqi, may choose a day for capping.
idiomatic: An edict proclaimed: "The Marquis of Yingdao, Yiqi, may fix a day for his capping.

literal: Let the outer offices follow the old practice in carrying it out.
idiomatic: Let the external offices arrange the ceremony according to former practice.

literal: He Zhen's abbreviated protocols for the capping rite and Wang Kan's privately compiled capping protocols were also domestic practices that could be followed.
idiomatic: He Zhen's summarized capping protocols and Wang Kan's privately drafted capping manual were likewise household guides that families could follow.

literal: In the fourth year of Zhengshi of Qi of Wei, Empress Zhen was established; the rite does not survive.
idiomatic: In the fourth year of Zhengshi under the Qi emperor of Wei, Empress Zhen was installed, but the ceremony itself has not survived.

literal: In the second year of Xianning of Emperor Wu of Jin, he presided at the hall and sent Grand Commandant Jia Chong to proclaim by document the establishment of Empress Yang—this was taking Empress Daohou.
idiomatic: In the second year of Xianning, Emperor Wu of Jin presided at the throne hall and sent Grand Commandant Jia Chong with a written appointment to establish Empress Yang—thus he took Empress Daohou as his consort.

literal: Thereupon a general amnesty was granted; dukes and princes and those below received gifts each according to rank.
idiomatic: A general amnesty followed, and princes, dukes, and all ranks below received gifts graded by station.

literal: The hundred officials presented congratulatory gifts.
idiomatic: The full body of officials presented congratulatory offerings.

literal: In the eighth year of Taikang, the responsible offices memorialized: "For the betrothal gift in the marriage rite, for a great marriage use dark and light silk, bundled silk plus a jade tablet, and horses two teams of four;
idiomatic: In the eighth year of Taikang, the responsible offices memorialized: "For the betrothal gifts in the marriage rite, a great marriage requires dark and red silk, bundled silk with a jade tablet, and two teams of four horses;

literal: For kings and marquises, dark and light silk, bundled silk plus a jade disk, riding horses;
idiomatic: For kings and marquises, dark and red silk, bundled silk with a jade disk, and riding horses;

literal: Great officers use dark and light silk, bundled silk plus a sheep.
idiomatic: Great officers should use dark and red silk, bundled silk with a sheep.

literal: In antiquity leather and horses served as court gifts; the Son of Heaven added a grain-pattern jade tablet, feudal lords added a great jade scepter.
idiomatic: In antiquity hides and horses served as the court offerings; the Son of Heaven added a grain-pattern jade tablet, and feudal lords added a great jade scepter.

literal: One may follow the Rites of Zhou and change the disk to a scepter; sheep, wild geese, wine, rice, and dark and light silk remain as before.
idiomatic: Following the Rites of Zhou, the jade disk may be replaced with a scepter; sheep, geese, wine, rice, and dark and red silk should remain unchanged.

literal: For feudal lords' marriage rites, add for the proposing-gifts, announcing the date, and the groom's arrival respectively five bolts of silk each, and for the betrothal gift four horses—all to be supplied by the groom's family, only the scepter to be prepared and delivered by the office.
idiomatic: For a feudal lord's marriage, five bolts of silk should be added for each of the proposing gifts, the announcement of the wedding date, and the groom's arrival, and four horses for the betrothal gift—all to be supplied by the groom's family, except the scepter, which the office should prepare and furnish.

literal: " Director of the Masters of Writing Zhu Zheng argued: "According to Wei precedent, for a prince taking a consort and a princess marrying, Son of Heaven and feudal lords used leather and horses as court gifts; the Son of Heaven added a grain-pattern jade tablet, feudal lords added a great jade scepter.
idiomatic: " Director of the Masters of Writing Zhu Zheng argued: "By Wei precedent, when a prince took a consort or a princess was given in marriage, the Son of Heaven and feudal lords used hides and horses as court gifts; the Son of Heaven added a grain-pattern jade tablet, and feudal lords a great jade scepter.

literal: Under Empress Gao of Han's rule, betrothal to an empress was two hundred jin of yellow gold and twelve horses;
idiomatic: Under Empress Dowager Gao of Han, betrothal to an empress required two hundred jin of yellow gold and twelve horses;

literal: For a lady of rank, fifty jin of gold and four horses.
idiomatic: for a consort of lower rank, fifty jin of gold and four horses.

literal: Under Wei, betrothal to an empress, a prince taking a consort, and a princess marrying used one hundred ninety bolts of silk.
idiomatic: Under Wei, betrothal to an empress, a prince's marriage, and a princess's wedding each required one hundred ninety bolts of silk.

literal: When Jin arose, precedent used three hundred bolts of silk.
idiomatic: When Jin came to power, precedent called for three hundred bolts of silk.

literal: " An edict said: "When a princess marries, the responsibility lies with the husband's clan; it is not fitting that all items be fully supplied; grant money sufficient and that is enough.
idiomatic: " An edict replied: "When a princess marries, her husband's family bears the burden; it is not right to supply every item in full—grant money enough to cover the cost and no more.

literal: Only provide the scepter; the rest follow precedent."
idiomatic: Provide only the scepter; let everything else follow established precedent."

literal: In the second year of Xiankang of Emperor Cheng, he presided at the hall and sent Concurrent Grand Guardian and General Who Leads the Army Zhuge Hui and Concurrent Grand Commandant and General Who Protects the Army Kong Yu with the six marriage gifts fully prepared to invest Empress Du.
idiomatic: In the second year of Xiankang, Emperor Cheng presided at the throne hall and sent Zhuge Hui, concurrently Grand Guardian and General Who Leads the Army, and Kong Yu, concurrently Grand Commandant and General Who Protects the Army, with the full complement of the six marriage gifts to invest Empress Du.

literal: That same day she entered the palace.
idiomatic: She entered the palace that same day.

literal: The emperor ascended the Hall of Supreme Ultimate and all ministers congratulated him—this was not ritual propriety.
idiomatic: The emperor then took his seat in the Hall of Supreme Ultimate, and the whole court congratulated him—conduct contrary to ritual.

literal: The marriage rite of a king—the rites contain no such regulation.
idiomatic: The marriage rite for a king appears nowhere in the canonical ritual texts.

literal: In the Spring and Autumn Annals, Duke Ji received his queen at Ji.
idiomatic: The Spring and Autumn Annals records that Duke Ji met his queen at Ji.

literal: The explanations of Guliang and Zuoshi differ again from Gongyang.
idiomatic: The Guliang and Zuoshi commentaries again disagree with the Gongyang tradition.

literal: Yet many Han and Wei precedents are abbreviated or missing.
idiomatic: Yet many Han and Wei precedents survive only in fragments or not at all.

literal: When Emperors Wu and Hui of Jin took empresses, under Jiangzuo there were again no ritual protocols, so when Emperor Cheng was about to take Empress Du, Minister of Ceremonies Hua Heng first joined with erudites to determine the rite.
idiomatic: After Emperors Wu and Hui took their empresses, the court south of the Yangzi had no surviving ritual manuals, so when Emperor Cheng was to take Empress Du, Minister of Ceremonies Hua Heng first worked with the erudites to fix the ceremony.

literal: Following Du Yu's Zuoshi Commentary view that the host of the marriage merely supplies the marriage gifts' offerings.
idiomatic: He relied on Du Yu's reading in the Zuoshi Commentary that the host of the marriage need only furnish the betrothal offerings.

literal: Also, King Ling of Zhou sought marriage from Qi; the Marquis of Qi asked Yan Huanzi, and Huanzi replied: "Of children born to husband and wife, so many persons; for paternal aunts and sisters, one says 'the surviving daughters left by the former lord So-and-So, so many persons.'
idiomatic: Again, when King Ling of Zhou sought a bride from Qi, the Marquis of Qi consulted Yan Huanzi, who answered: "Of the children born to husband and wife, so many; for paternal aunts and sisters, one says, 'The surviving daughters left by the late Lord Such-and-Such, so many.'

literal: " This shows the Son of Heaven's command can descend directly, and the minister's reply can go straight upward.
idiomatic: " This shows that the Son of Heaven's command could pass straight down, and a minister's reply could pass straight up.

literal: Earlier Confucians held that Qiu Ming recorded the affair in detail probably because it was the marriage rite of a king.
idiomatic: Earlier scholars thought Zuo Qiuming set the matter down in detail because it illustrated a king's marriage rite.

literal: Therefore Emperor Cheng presided at the hall and sent envoys proclaiming by imperial order to invest the empress.
idiomatic: Accordingly, Emperor Cheng presided at the throne hall and sent envoys with an imperial proclamation to invest the empress.

literal: Yet its ritual protocols again are not fully preserved.
idiomatic: Yet even those ritual protocols were not fully preserved.

literal: In the first year of Jianyuan of Emperor Kang, Empress Chu was taken.
idiomatic: In the first year of Jianyuan under Emperor Kang, Empress Chu was brought into the palace.

literal: Yet in the protocols the steps did not set up the maotou.
idiomatic: Yet the written protocols called for no maotou figures to be posted on the steps.

literal: The Palace Censor memorialized: "Now receiving the empress—following how Empress Cheng Gong entered the palace with imperial objects, yet the protocols have the supreme lord in dragon robe and cap ascending the hall with maotou not set up—seek clarification.
idiomatic: The Palace Censor memorialized: "In receiving the empress now, we should follow Empress Cheng Gong's entry with the imperial regalia at hand; yet the protocols have the sovereign ascending in full dragon robe and cap while no maotou are posted on the steps. We ask how this is to be handled.

literal: Also examining the past reception of Empress Gong, only the Azure Dragon banner was made; the rest were simply imperial objects at hand.
idiomatic: Moreover, when Empress Gong was received in the past, only the Azure Dragon banner was newly made; everything else was drawn from items already kept in the palace.

literal: Now we should preside at the hall and send envoys, yet set up the Five Ox banners and flags, with maotou and bihan all brought out.
idiomatic: Now we are to preside at the throne hall and dispatch envoys, yet also erect the Five Ox banners and bring out the maotou and bihan as well.

literal: To follow the old system immediately—now it is lacking.
idiomatic: If we are to follow the old system at once, the needed implements are now lacking.

literal: " An edict said: "The reason for ascending the Hall of Supreme Ultimate in proper ritual dress is to honor the beginning, and therefore complete the rite.
idiomatic: " An edict replied: "The sovereign ascends the Hall of Supreme Ultimate in full ceremonial dress to show reverence at the beginning of the rite, and therefore every proper emblem should be in place.

literal: Now why should what is important be omitted and legal ritual objects withdrawn?
idiomatic: Why now omit what matters most and strip away the ritual objects prescribed by law?

literal: Also, when Empress Gong's spirit tablet entered the temple, the former emperor decreed that empress ritual should be reduced and the Five Ox banner should not be erected—yet now it is set up again!
idiomatic: Again, when Empress Gong's spirit tablet was installed in the temple, the late emperor decreed that an empress's rites should be reduced and the Five Ox banner should not be raised—yet now it is to be raised again!

literal: Since the Five Ox banner is not to be set up, the implements for maotou and bihan are easy to supply.
idiomatic: If the Five Ox banner is not erected, the maotou and bihan can easily be supplied.

literal: " Another edict said: "Since the old system is hard to follow exactly, and to prepare it all now is also not fitting.
idiomatic: " A further edict said: "Since the old system cannot be followed exactly, and assembling it all at once would be improper even now,

literal: Treasury stores should serve only military and state expenses.
idiomatic: the treasury's stores should be reserved only for military and state needs.

literal: Let legal dress and ritual adornments be roughly provided; stop the rest of the duplicate miscellaneous implements."
idiomatic: Provide ceremonial dress and ornaments in rough form, and suspend the rest of the duplicate and miscellaneous implements."

literal: When it came to the first year of Shengping of Emperor Mu, when Empress He was to be taken, Minister of Ceremonies Wang Biaozhi first drew more extensively on classics, commentaries, and various precedents to correct the rite, deeply contrary to Gongyang's meaning that the marriage rite does not name a host.
idiomatic: By the first year of Shengping under Emperor Mu, when Empress He was to be taken, Minister of Ceremonies Wang Biaozhi drew more widely on the classics, commentaries, and precedents to set the rite right, in sharp opposition to the Gongyang view that a royal marriage should not name a host.

literal: He also said: "The king toward the four seas—none are not subjects and concubines.
idiomatic: He argued further: "Toward all within the four seas, the king has no one who is not subject or consort.

literal: Even kin who are father or elder brother, worthies who are teacher or friend—all are pure subjects.
idiomatic: Even a father or elder brother by blood, or a teacher or friend of virtue, are wholly his subjects.

literal: In revering the beginning of the Three Bonds to fix the order of Heaven and Earth, how can there be the dignity of a Heaven-father yet speak of a subject's command to take a spouse;
idiomatic: In upholding the Three Bonds that establish the order of Heaven and Earth, how can one who bears Heaven's dignity speak as though a subject's command were needed to take a spouse?

literal: How can there be the baseness of a subject yet speak the Heaven-father's name to perform the great rite.
idiomatic: And how can a subject, low in station, speak in the name of Heaven's father to conduct the great rite?

literal: Searching far in ancient ritual, there is no such regulation for a king;
idiomatic: Searching the distant past in the ritual canon, no king had such a rule;

literal: Searching near in historical records, there is no such parallel for a king.
idiomatic: consulting recent historical records, no king had such a precedent.

literal: In feeling it is unsettling; in principle it does not cohere.
idiomatic: It is emotionally troubling and logically untenable.

literal: Examine the second year of Xianning, when Empress Daohou was taken: the Dowager Empress of Hongxun as mother ruled the realm, yet there was no text appointing a kinsman minister as host of marriage for Emperor Wu's father or elder brother.
idiomatic: Consider the second year of Xianning, when Empress Daohou was taken: though the Dowager Empress of Hongxun, as mother, ruled the realm, no document appointed a kinsman or minister to serve as marriage host on behalf of Emperor Wu's father or elder brother.

literal: Also examine what Great Jin had already carried out: the Xianning precedent did not name father, elder brother, teacher, or friend—so what Hua Heng submitted at Xiankang accorded with the old.
idiomatic: Review what Great Jin had already done: the Xianning precedent named no father, elder brother, teacher, or friend—so Hua Heng's Xiankang proposal accorded with established practice.

literal: Your servant foolishly holds that today's empress-taking protocols should uniformly follow the Xiankang precedent.
idiomatic: Your servant humbly submits that the present empress-taking ceremony should follow the Xiankang precedent in full.

literal: " Thereupon it was adopted.
idiomatic: " The court accepted his recommendation.

literal: The six marriage gifts Hua Heng fixed said one should follow Han antiquity and what Great Jin had already practiced—Heng still knew earlier affairs, so Wang Biaozhi largely followed Xiankang for this reason.
idiomatic: In fixing the six marriage gifts, Hua Heng had urged adherence to Han custom and to what Great Jin had already done; because Heng still remembered earlier practice, Wang Biaozhi chiefly followed the Xiankang model for that reason.

literal: Only because the household taking a wife should not raise music for three days, while Xiankang's ministers congratulating was ritual error;
idiomatic: Only on one point did he dissent: the bride's household should keep silence and refrain from music for three days, whereas the ministers' congratulations at Xiankang had been a breach of ritual;

literal: Therefore only the Xianning gift-presentation rite was followed, and congratulations were not repeated.
idiomatic: so he kept only the Xianning gift presentation and omitted the congratulatory ceremony.

literal: The temple announcement, six-gift document texts, and other rites were all fixed by Biaozhi.
idiomatic: The announcement to the temple, the texts for the six marriage gifts, and the rest of the ceremony were all settled by Biaozhi.

literal: Examining in detail there are canonical regulations; the proposing-gifts document imperial writing says: "The emperor consults the former Grand Commandant's staff officer He Qi: from the origin of primordial Heaven, establishing human relations, extending to husband and wife, to serve Heaven and Earth, the ancestral temples, and the altars of soil and grain—counsel was taken of dukes and ministers, all holding it fitting to follow the old canon.
idiomatic: On close examination the canonical forms prescribe the following. The proposing-gifts document, bearing the imperial seal, reads: "The emperor addresses the former staff officer of the Grand Commandant, He Qi: from the origin of primordial Heaven, when human relations were first ordered, down to husband and wife joined to serve Heaven and Earth, the ancestral temples, and the altars of soil and grain, the dukes and ministers were consulted, and all agreed that the old canon should be followed.

literal: Now send the bearer of credentials Minister of Ceremonies Biaozhi and Director of the Imperial Clan Zong with ritual to present proposing gifts.
idiomatic: We now send Minister of Ceremonies Biaozhi, bearer of credentials, and Director of the Imperial Clan Zong to present the proposing gifts according to ritual.

literal: " The host says: "The emperor's gracious command seeks marriage with our humble clan; full measure of selection by proposing gifts.
idiomatic: " The host replies: "The emperor's gracious command seeks a bride from our humble house; the full rite of selection by proposing gifts is hereby acknowledged.

literal: Your servant's second cousin, the late Gentleman of the Palace Horse with Golden Saddle Zhunzhi's surviving daughter—unpracticed in instruction, of such-and-such stature in dress and shoes—reverently receives the old regulations and respectfully obeys the canonical system.
idiomatic: My second cousin once removed, the late Gentleman of the Golden Saddle, Zhunzhi, left a daughter who is still young in training, of modest stature in dress and carriage; in reverent obedience to the old regulations and canonical order, she is offered for your choice.

literal: The former Grand Commandant's staff officer, Marquis of Duxiang, subject on humble soil He Qi kowtows twice and receives the imperial edict.
idiomatic: The former staff officer of the Grand Commandant, Marquis of Duxiang, your subject on humble soil, He Qi, kowtows twice and receives the imperial command.

literal: " Next the ask-name document text says: "The emperor says: I consult Official So-and-So of Clan Such-and-Such—the two principles paired, receiving Heaven's ordering of things, established in the inner position, one must await a fine clan; weightily manifest the old canon.
idiomatic: " The next ask-name document reads: "The emperor says: I address Official Such-and-Such of the Such-and-Such clan. Heaven and Earth joined in harmony sustain all things; she who is established within must come from a worthy house. Let the old canon be honored once more.

literal: Now send the bearer of credentials Minister of Ceremonies So-and-So and Director of the Imperial Clan So-and-So with ritual to ask the name.
idiomatic: We now send Minister of Ceremonies Such-and-Such, bearer of credentials, and Director of the Imperial Clan Such-and-Such to ask her name according to ritual.
